summary: Describes the format of an LDAP URL, which spells out an LDAP search to fetch information from a directory, or points to a service where an operation can continue, such as in a referral. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: An LDAP URL packs a whole directory query into one string: which server to ask, which entry to start from, how deep to search, what to look for and which attributes to return. It is also the format used for the pointers a directory server sends back when it wants you to ask a different server.

questions: what is a critical extension in an ldap url
subtitle: How to write an LDAP search, or a pointer to an LDAP server, as a single URL.

tldr.problem: An LDAP search needs a server, a base entry, a scope, a filter and a list of attributes. Writing all of that out by hand every time is clumsy, and there was no agreed way to write it as one string.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the LDAP URL: a string that begins with the scheme ldap and carries the host, port, distinguished name, attributes, scope, filter and extensions in a fixed order, with defaults for anything left out.
tldr.outcome: A whole directory search can be written as one line, and the same format is used for the pointers a server returns when it wants a client to go elsewhere. The document replaced RFC 2255 in 2006.

today: RFC 4516 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2255 in 2006, updating the grammar to use the productions of RFC 3986, adding the defaults section and the extensions mechanism, and removing the bind name extension, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510.

sections.title: What an LDAP URL Is
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. This document specifies the LDAP URL format for version 3 of LDAP and clarifies how LDAP URLs are resolved. It also defines an extension mechanism for LDAP URLs, which may be used to provide access to new LDAP extensions.

An LDAP URL describes an LDAP search operation used to retrieve information from an LDAP directory. In the context of a referral or a reference, it describes a service where an LDAP operation may be progressed instead.

Two limits are worth stating. Not all the parameters of the LDAP search operation described in RFC 4511 can be expressed in this format. And URLs may be used to represent reference knowledge, including knowledge for operations that are not searches. The document is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification, RFC 4510, which in turn obsoleted RFC 3377 in its entirety. It replaces RFC 2255.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory query has a lot of parts, so the document gives them a single written form. It is a one-way format: not every possible search can be written this way.

sections.title: The URL Format
sections.content:
An LDAP URL begins with the protocol prefix ldap and follows the grammar in the ABNF notation of RFC 4234. The scheme is followed by two slashes, then an optional host and optional port, then a slash and the distinguished name, and then up to four question-mark-separated fields: the attributes, the scope, the filter and the extensions.

The host may contain literal IPv6 addresses. The distinguished name is in the string format of RFC 4514 and identifies the base object of the search, or the target of a non-search operation. The attributes field says which attributes should be returned. The scope says how far the search reaches: base for the base object only, one for one level down, or sub for the whole subtree. The filter is the search filter, in the format of RFC 4515. The extensions field carries the extensibility mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The order of the fields never changes: server, then entry, then what to return, then how deep, then what to match, then extras. Each field is separated by a question mark.

sections.title: Extensions and Criticality
sections.content:
The extensions construct is a simple comma-separated list of type=value pairs, where the value part may be omitted for options that do not need one. Each pair is a separate extension, and the LDAP URL extensions are not necessarily related to any of the LDAP extension mechanisms. An extension may be supported or unsupported by the client resolving the URL.

An extension prefixed with the exclamation mark, ASCII 0x21, is critical; one without it is non-critical. If an implementation understands an extension and can use it, it must make use of it. If an extension is not implemented and is marked critical, the implementation must not process the URL at all. If an extension is not implemented and is not marked critical, the implementation must ignore it.

The extension type may be given as a numeric object identifier, for example 1.2.3.4, or in the descriptive form, for example myLDAPURLExtension, though the descriptive form should be restricted to registered descriptive names. No LDAP URL extensions are defined in this document; other documents or a future version may define one or more.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra behaviour can be bolted onto a URL. An extension marked with an exclamation mark is a demand: if the client cannot do it, it must not follow the URL at all. An unmarked one is a hint that can be ignored.

sections.title: Percent-Encoding
sections.content:
A generated LDAP URL must consist only of the restricted set of characters in the reserved, unreserved or percent-encoded productions of RFC 3986. Implementations should accept other valid UTF-8 strings as input.

An octet must be percent-encoded in any of three situations. It must be encoded when it is neither in the reserved set nor in the unreserved set of RFC 3986. It must be encoded when it is the single reserved character ? and occurs inside a distinguished name, a filter or another element of the URL. And it must be encoded when it is a comma that occurs inside an extension value. The two escaping schemes interact: the LDAP filter escaping character, the backslash, is itself written as %5c in the URL, so the filter for three null bytes and a control character appears as (four-octet=%5c00%5c00%5c00%5c04).

Before percent-encoding is applied, the extensions component of the URL may contain one or more null bytes. No other component may.
sections.plainLanguage: Spaces and other awkward characters are written as a percent sign and two hex digits. A question mark inside a name is written that way so it is not mistaken for a field separator.

sections.title: Defaults for Missing Fields
sections.content:
Some fields of the LDAP URL are optional, and the document gives a default for each when it is absent. Other documents may specify different defaulting rules; for example, Section 4.1.10 of RFC 4511 gives a different rule for the correct distinguished name to use when it is absent from an LDAP URL returned as a referral.

If no host is given, the client must have some prior knowledge of an appropriate LDAP server to contact. The default port is TCP port 389. If no distinguished name is given, the default is the zero-length DN. If the attributes part is omitted, all user attributes of the entry or entries should be requested, either by setting the attributes field of the LDAP search request to a NULL list or by using the special all-user-attributes selector, which is written as an asterisk. If the scope is omitted, a scope of base is assumed. If the filter is omitted, a filter of (objectClass=*) is assumed. If the extensions are omitted, no extensions are assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: Leave out a field and the document says what it means. No host means the client has to know one already, no port means 389, and no filter means everything matches.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The simplest examples point at the entry for the University of Michigan, first at a server of the client's choosing and then at a named server: ldap:///o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US and ldap://ldap1.example.net/o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US. Both are base object searches of that entry with the filter (objectClass=*) and all attributes requested.

Adding a field asks for one attribute only, ldap://ldap1.example.net/o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US?postalAddress. A subtree search on a server at port 6666 for any entry with the common name "Babs Jensen" is written ldap://ldap1.example.net:6666/o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US??sub?(cn=Babs%20Jensen). The children of the c=GB entry are LDAP://ldap1.example.com/c=GB?objectClass?ONE.

A question mark inside a name is percent-encoded, giving ldap://ldap2.example.com/o=Question%3f,c=US?mail. A backslash inside a filter is escaped twice over, in LDAP and then in the URL. A comma inside a distinguished name is written %5C2C. Three URLs that differ only in their trailing characters are equivalent: ldap://ldap.example.net, ldap://ldap.example.net/ and ldap://ldap.example.net/?, and all three point at the root DSE of that server. The last two examples show the same hypothetical bind name extension written once as an ordinary extension and once with the exclamation mark that makes it critical.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples build up a URL field by field, and then show the escaping rules in practice: a space, a question mark and a comma all written as percent codes so they cannot be mistaken for structure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general URL security considerations of RFC 3986 apply to LDAP URLs, and the use of security mechanisms when processing them needs particular care, because clients may meet many different servers through URLs and URLs are likely to be processed automatically without user intervention. A client should have a user-configurable policy that controls which servers it will open LDAP sessions with and with which security mechanisms, and should not open sessions that are inconsistent with that policy. If a client reuses an existing session when resolving a URL, it must ensure that the session is compatible with the URL and that no security policy is violated.

Sending authentication information may violate a user's privacy requirements, so in the absence of a policy permitting it a client should use an anonymous LDAP session. Simply opening a transport connection to another server may also violate privacy requirements, so clients should give the user a way to control URL processing. Reusable passwords may reveal easily abused information to the remote server or to eavesdroppers and should not be used unless policy explicitly permits them; strong authentication methods that reveal nothing sensitive are much preferred, and if the URL represents a referral for an update operation, strong authentication should be used.

Following an LDAP URL may cause unexpected results, for example retrieving large amounts of data or starting a long-lived search. The security implications of resolving an LDAP URL are the same as those of resolving an LDAP search query.
sections.plainLanguage: A URL can send a client to a new server without asking, so the client should have a policy about which servers it is willing to talk to and should not leak credentials along the way. Following a URL can also pull back a lot of data, so it carries the same risk as any other search.

data.title: ldapurl
data.code:
ldapurl = scheme COLON SLASH SLASH [host [COLON port]]
           [SLASH dn [QUESTION [attributes]
           [QUESTION [scope] [QUESTION [filter]
           [QUESTION extensions]]]]]

scope    = "base" / "one" / "sub"
extension = [EXCLAMATION] extype [EQUALS exvalue]
extype   = oid

items.title: Host
items.text: The client must already know which server to contact.

items.title: Attributes
items.text: All user attributes of the entry or entries.

Extra options. The exclamation mark makes one critical.
